questions.q: What does running `aws configure` actually do?
options: Installs the AWS Console as a desktop application
Creates a brand-new IAM user in your AWS account automatically
Deploys a default S3 bucket and EC2 instance for you
Writes your access key ID, secret access key, default region, and output format to files under ~/.aws/, which every later CLI command reads from
questions.explain: aws configure sets up local credential and config files that every subsequent aws command relies on.

questions.q: What is the general shape of every AWS CLI command, per this lesson?
options: aws <service> <action> [parameters] — e.g. aws s3 cp, aws glue start-job-run
aws --run <script-file>
There is no consistent shape; every command is structured differently
aws <region> <account-id> <resource-name>
questions.explain: Every command follows service then action then parameters, and that pair maps closely onto a policy's Action field.

questions.q: What determines whether a given aws CLI command succeeds or returns AccessDenied?
options: Whether the command was typed in uppercase or lowercase
The version number of the AWS CLI tool installed locally
The IAM identity (user or role) whose credentials are configured — its attached policies decide which actions are allowed, per Chapter 3
AccessDenied only ever happens due to network connectivity issues
questions.explain: The CLI is just a client — the actual permissions decision happens against whichever IAM identity's credentials are active, exactly as covered in the IAM chapter.

questions.q: Why is `aws s3 sync` especially useful for a data engineer compared to `aws s3 cp` on a folder?
options: sync only transfers files that are new or changed, which matters once a folder contains thousands of files
sync deletes the entire destination bucket before every run
There is no functional difference between sync and cp
sync is the only command that can upload to S3 at all
questions.explain: sync is the efficient choice for whole-folder transfers because it skips files that haven't changed.

questions.q: What happens if you forget the --profile flag when you have multiple named profiles configured?
options: The AWS CLI refuses to run any command until a profile is explicitly specified
The command silently falls back to the [default] profile, which can touch the wrong AWS account without an obvious error
AWS automatically detects which account you intended to use
Named profiles are merged together into one combined identity
questions.explain: This silent fallback to [default] is called out explicitly as a common source of confusion when juggling multiple identities.
